questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which type of adverse drug reaction is dose-dependent, predictable from the drug's pharmacology and accounts for most reactions in practice?
questions.concept: Type A reactions are managed by dose reduction whereas type B idiosyncratic reactions require withdrawal, and this distinction determines whether the drug can ever be used again in that patient.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which reporting system in India collects spontaneous reports of suspected adverse drug reactions?
options: The Pharmacovigilance Programme of India, coordinated by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation trials registry
The Drug Controller General of India licensing database
questions.concept: Spontaneous reporting detects rare and delayed reactions that trials are too small and too short to find, which is why post-marketing surveillance is a distinct phase of drug evaluation.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampicin and the international normalised ratio falls. The mechanism and the time course are:
options: Induction of CYP2C9 with the effect developing over days to weeks as new enzyme is synthesised
Inhibition of CYP2C9 with an immediate effect
Displacement from plasma protein with an immediate effect
questions.concept: Induction requires new protein synthesis so both the onset and the offset are gradual, which is why the dose must be adjusted again when the inducer is stopped.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on a statin develops myopathy after starting clarithromycin. The mechanism is:
options: Inhibition of CYP3A4 raising statin concentrations
questions.concept: Enzyme inhibition is immediate because it is competitive, and the risk is greatest with simvastatin and atorvastatin while pravastatin and rosuvastatin are less CYP3A4 dependent.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does a drug with a narrow therapeutic index and a high hepatic extraction ratio show the greatest change in effect when an enzyme inhibitor is added?
options: First-pass metabolism is a large fraction of the dose, so inhibiting it markedly raises bioavailability
questions.concept: This is why oral drugs such as verapamil, midazolam and simvastatin are so susceptible to interactions with grapefruit juice and azole antifungals.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does a drug that causes a type B idiosyncratic reaction usually escape detection in phase III trials?
options: Reactions occurring in fewer than 1 in 1000 patients require far more exposures than a trial enrols
The reaction only occurs after 10 years
Trials do not record adverse events
questions.concept: The rule of three states that to be reasonably confident of seeing at least one event of a given frequency about three times its reciprocal must be exposed, which is why post-marketing surveillance is indispensable.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adverse Drug Effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which receptor mediates bronchodilatation, and which drug is selective for it?
questions.concept: Beta-2 selectivity is relative and is lost at high dose, which is why tremor, tachycardia and hypokalaemia appear when nebulised doses are escalated in acute asthma.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is a selective alpha-1 antagonist used in benign prostatic hyperplasia with relative uroselectivity?
questions.concept: Its preference for the alpha-1A subtype in prostatic smooth muscle causes less postural hypotension than prazosin, and the first-dose phenomenon is the classic hazard of the non-selective agents.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which effect explains why adrenaline is preferred to noradrenaline in anaphylaxis?
options: It combines alpha-1 vasoconstriction with beta-2 bronchodilatation and mast cell stabilisation
It is a pure alpha agonist
questions.concept: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh gives faster and more reliable absorption than subcutaneous, and the dose is 0.5 mg of the 1 in 1000 solution in an adult.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which effect of a non-selective beta blocker explains its danger in a diabetic on insulin?
options: It masks the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia and impairs glycogenolytic recovery
questions.concept: Sweating remains because it is cholinergically mediated, so it becomes the only warning symptom, and cardioselective agents are preferred where a beta blocker is needed.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which paradoxical effect follows the use of adrenaline in a patient fully treated with a non-selective beta blocker?
options: A rise in blood pressure with reflex bradycardia from unopposed alpha stimulation
questions.concept: The same principle explains why alpha blockade must precede beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma, and why beta blockers are avoided in cocaine toxicity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug acts as an indirectly acting sympathomimetic and shows tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing?
options: Ephedrine, through displacement of stored noradrenaline
questions.concept: Depletion of releasable stores together with receptor desensitisation explains the rapid loss of effect, in contrast to the slow tolerance seen with directly acting agents.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does a patient on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor develop a hypertensive crisis after eating mature cheese?
options: Tyramine escapes gut and hepatic metabolism, enters sympathetic nerves and displaces a large amount of stored noradrenaline
questions.concept: The reversible selective inhibitor moclobemide and the transdermal selegiline patch largely avoid the reaction, which is why the dietary restriction is specific to the older irreversible non-selective agents.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Adrenergic System

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which anthelmintic acts by inhibiting microtubule polymerisation through binding beta-tubulin?
questions.concept: Because it depletes the worm's energy stores over days it is given as a short course, and the same mechanism explains its teratogenic potential and the need to avoid it in the first trimester.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is the treatment of choice for neurocysticercosis, and what must accompany it?
options: Albendazole with corticosteroids and antiepileptics to control the inflammatory response to dying cysts
questions.concept: Killing the cysts provokes oedema and seizures, so steroid cover is essential, and ophthalmic cysticercosis must be excluded first because intraocular inflammation can destroy vision.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antiamoebic acts only in the intestinal lumen and is used to eradicate cysts after treating invasive disease?
questions.concept: Tissue amoebicides such as metronidazole do not reliably clear luminal cysts, so a luminal agent must follow to prevent relapse and interrupt transmission.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is used for filariasis and causes a Mazzotti-type reaction from dying microfilariae, requiring caution in onchocerciasis?
questions.concept: In onchocerciasis the reaction can threaten sight, so ivermectin is used instead, and combining diethylcarbamazine with albendazole is the mass treatment strategy for lymphatic filariasis.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antileprotic drug causes reddish-brown skin discolouration and has an anti-inflammatory action useful in erythema nodosum leprosum?
questions.concept: It is a riminophenazine dye that binds mycobacterial DNA, and its pigmentation is reversible but is a common cause of poor adherence, particularly in lighter-skinned patients.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why is metronidazole combined with an alcohol warning, and what is the mechanism?
options: It inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, producing a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, vomiting and hypotension
It causes hepatotoxicity with alcohol only
questions.concept: Its reduction to a cytotoxic nitro radical by anaerobic organisms is its antimicrobial mechanism, which also explains why it is inactive against aerobes.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Anthelmintic and Antiamoebic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antibiotic class inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and is the drug of choice for atypical pneumonia?
questions.concept: Because Mycoplasma has no cell wall, beta-lactams are useless, and macrolides also cover Legionella and Chlamydophila, which is why they are combined with a beta-lactam for severe community-acquired pneumonia.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which pharmacodynamic property makes once-daily aminoglycoside dosing both effective and safer?
options: Concentration-dependent killing with a prolonged post-antibiotic effect, while toxicity relates to trough exposure
Toxicity relating to peak level only
questions.concept: Beta-lactams by contrast show time-dependent killing, so their efficacy depends on the time above the minimum inhibitory concentration, favouring frequent dosing or extended infusion.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antibiotic is the drug of choice for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia?
options: Vancomycin, with daptomycin as an alternative
questions.concept: Trough monitoring or area under the curve targeting guides dosing because the therapeutic window is narrow, and treatment failure with a rising minimum inhibitory concentration prompts a switch.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains resistance to fluoroquinolones?
options: Mutations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV with efflux pump upregulation
questions.concept: Because resistance emerges stepwise under selection pressure, restricting fluoroquinolone use is a stewardship priority, and their association with tendinopathy and aortic events has further narrowed indications.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antibiotic combination is synergistic against enterococcal endocarditis, and why?
options: Ampicillin with gentamicin, because cell wall disruption enhances aminoglycoside uptake
questions.concept: Enterococci are intrinsically tolerant to cell wall agents alone, and high-level aminoglycoside resistance abolishes the synergy, which is why it must be tested for before relying on the combination.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which adverse effect limits the use of chloramphenicol, and which is dose-independent?
options: Idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia, which is dose-independent, in addition to dose-related marrow suppression
questions.concept: Grey baby syndrome in neonates results from immature glucuronidation, and these hazards confine its use largely to topical preparations and to specific situations such as typhoid or rickettsial disease where alternatives are unavailable.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does the presence of an inducible AmpC beta-lactamase make a third-generation cephalosporin unreliable even when the isolate tests susceptible?
options: Therapy can select derepressed mutants, so susceptibility is lost during treatment
The organism has no cell wall
The enzyme is inhibited by clavulanate
questions.concept: Organisms such as Serratia, Pseudomonas, indole-positive Proteus, Citrobacter and Enterobacter carry this risk, so carbapenems or cefepime are preferred for serious infection.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antimicrobial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which laboratory test monitors unfractionated heparin, and which antidote reverses it?
options: Activated partial thromboplastin time, reversed by protamine sulphate
Prothrombin time, reversed by vitamin K
Thrombin time, reversed by fresh frozen plasma
questions.concept: Low molecular weight heparin requires no routine monitoring and is only partially reversed by protamine, which is one reason unfractionated heparin is preferred where reversibility matters.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antiplatelet drug irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 for the life of the platelet?
questions.concept: Because platelets cannot synthesise new enzyme, the effect lasts 7 to 10 days, which determines the interval needed before surgery, whereas endothelial cells regenerate cyclooxygenase within hours.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which agent reverses the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran?
questions.concept: Andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors rivaroxaban and apixaban, so matching the reversal agent to the drug class is essential in major bleeding.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the delayed onset of warfarin's anticoagulant effect?
options: Existing carboxylated clotting factors must be cleared, and factor II has a half-life of about 60 hours
questions.concept: The transient early fall in protein C, which has a short half-life, explains warfarin-induced skin necrosis and the need for heparin overlap in acute thrombosis.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antiplatelet mechanism does clopidogrel use, and what pharmacogenetic factor limits its effect?
options: Irreversible P2Y12 receptor blockade, requiring CYP2C19 activation which is impaired in poor metabolisers
questions.concept: Prasugrel and ticagrelor are less dependent on CYP2C19, and proton pump inhibitors that inhibit the enzyme may reduce clopidogrel effect, which is why pantoprazole is often preferred.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does a statin lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol more when given at night for the shorter-acting agents?
options: Cholesterol synthesis peaks overnight, so inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase then matches the diurnal rhythm
The receptor is only expressed at night
questions.concept: Longer-acting agents such as atorvastatin and rosuvastatin can be given at any time because their half-lives exceed the diurnal cycle, which improves adherence.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs Affecting Coagulation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antihypertensive class is preferred as first line in a young patient with proteinuric chronic kidney disease?
options: An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker
questions.concept: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure and reduces proteinuria beyond the effect of blood pressure reduction, which is why an expected small early rise in creatinine is accepted.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which adverse effect is characteristic of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers?
options: Ankle oedema from precapillary vasodilatation without venodilatation
questions.concept: Because the oedema is not from fluid retention it responds poorly to diuretics and better to dose reduction or to combining with a renin-angiotensin blocker, which dilates the venous side.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antihypertensive is safest in pregnancy and has the longest record of use?
questions.concept: Labetalol and nifedipine are also used, whereas renin-angiotensin blockers are fetotoxic in the second and third trimesters and atenolol has been associated with growth restriction.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which combination should be avoided because it increases the risk of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury without added benefit?
options: An ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
An ACE inhibitor with a thiazide
A calcium channel blocker with a thiazide
A beta blocker with a calcium channel blocker of the dihydropyridine class
questions.concept: Dual renin-angiotensin blockade was shown in ONTARGET and ALTITUDE to increase harm, so the axis is blocked at only one point.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the antihypertensive action of spironolactone in resistant hypertension?
options: Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade, which addresses the frequent contribution of aldosterone excess
questions.concept: The PATHWAY-2 trial showed spironolactone to be the most effective fourth-line agent, reflecting how often unrecognised primary aldosteronism underlies resistant hypertension.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, so it is given with a beta blocker and a diuretic?
questions.concept: It also causes a drug-induced lupus syndrome with anti-histone antibodies, more often in slow acetylators, which limits long-term use outside pregnancy and heart failure regimens.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does abrupt withdrawal of clonidine cause rebound hypertension?
options: Upregulated peripheral adrenergic responsiveness is unmasked when central alpha-2 inhibition is removed, releasing a catecholamine surge
It has a very long half-life
questions.concept: The drug must therefore be tapered, and if a crisis occurs it is treated by reinstating clonidine or by combined alpha and beta blockade rather than beta blockade alone.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Antihypertensive Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antidepressant class is first line because of a favourable safety profile in overdose?
questions.concept: Tricyclic overdose causes seizures, coma and cardiac arrhythmia from sodium channel blockade, which is why they are avoided where suicidal risk is significant.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mental Illness

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antipsychotic requires mandatory monitoring of the neutrophil count, and for which adverse effect?
questions.concept: Clozapine is uniquely effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reduces suicidality, so the monitoring requirement is accepted, and myocarditis, seizures and severe constipation are its other serious risks.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mental Illness

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the delay of two to four weeks before an antidepressant produces clinical benefit?
options: Downregulation of presynaptic autoreceptors and downstream neuroplastic changes take weeks despite immediate reuptake blockade
Slow accumulation to steady state alone
questions.concept: Because the biochemical effect is immediate but the clinical effect is not, patients must be warned and monitored, since early activation may precede mood improvement.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mental Illness

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why must a washout period be observed when switching from fluoxetine to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor?
options: Norfluoxetine has a half-life of one to two weeks, so serotonin syndrome can occur unless five weeks elapse
questions.concept: Serotonin syndrome presents with altered mental state, autonomic instability and neuromuscular hyperactivity with clonus and hyperreflexia, which distinguishes it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome with lead-pipe rigidity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mental Illness

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Why does lithium toxicity occur when a thiazide or an NSAID is added?
options: Both reduce renal lithium clearance, thiazides by increasing proximal reabsorption and NSAIDs by reducing renal perfusion
questions.concept: Lithium is not protein bound and is entirely renally excreted, so anything that alters sodium handling or glomerular filtration changes its level, which is why levels are checked after any such change.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology 8e, Ch. Drugs for Mental Illness
